title: The Exercises
hook: a month-long retreat in four weeks, guided by a director

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Dominican day at home, and our last day with Dominic's family. Your line was pray, study, share. What one true thing did you hand on, and to whom? Day one thousand two hundred fifty.

Here is a strange kind of book. Its author didn't write it for you to read. It's thin, full of numbered notes, lists, instructions, and suggestions for what to do next. Read it straight through, cover to cover, and it can feel like reading the rules of a sport you've never played. That's because it isn't a book to read. It's a book to use, by one person guiding another. The author was a Spanish soldier turned pilgrim named Ignatius of Loyola, and the friends who gathered around him became the Jesuits, the new family on our path today. The book is where they start. Today's word is its name.
screen: `A BOOK NOT MEANT TO BE READ.` → `IGNATIUS OF LOYOLA.` → `THE JESUITS BEGIN HERE.`

segments.voice: The Spiritual Exercises begin by explaining the name. Ignatius says: just as walking, marching and running are exercises for the body, so these are exercises for the soul, every way of preparing it to let go of disordered attachments, and then to seek and find what God wants for a life. Exercise, not information. You don't get fit reading about push-ups. The full retreat lasts about a month, kept in quiet, and it's divided into four parts Ignatius calls weeks. They aren't calendar weeks. They're stages, and a person may spend longer in one than another. In the first, the retreatant faces their own failures and God's mercy. In the second, they walk with Christ through his life. In the third, through his passion. In the fourth, they stay with the risen Christ. And no one makes this alone. The book is written for a director, a guide who meets the retreatant each day, offers the next exercise, listens, and adjusts. Ignatius even allows the Exercises to be made in daily life, a little each day over a longer time, for someone who can't leave home for a month. Why does a quiet month matter? Jesus does something like it with his friends. After they come back from a busy mission, he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little." Apart, so you can hear. Exercises for the soul are like any training: they need time set aside, and someone in your corner.
screen: `WALKING AND RUNNING TRAIN THE BODY.` · `FOUR WEEKS: STAGES, NOT CALENDAR.` · `A DIRECTOR GUIDES EACH DAY.` · `OR IN DAILY LIFE, LITTLE BY LITTLE.` · then, large: `COME APART INTO A DESERT PLACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a quiet day. Not today, necessarily. Settle, and breathe. Look at the weeks ahead and find one day, or half a day, or even two free hours, that you could set apart. Picture where you'd go: a park bench, a church, a library, a quiet room with the phone in a drawer. Picture what you'd bring: a notebook, a Gospel, nothing at all. Picture who might be your guide, a friend or a priest you could talk to after. Hold that plan in the quiet. If you pray, you can offer that day ahead of time. The bell holds the time.
Spiritual Exercises. Ignatius's handbook for a guided retreat in four stages he calls weeks: training for the soul, the way walking and running train the body. Today's word.
Your line: exercises for the soul. Today, put your quiet day on the calendar, with a time and a place, the way you'd book any training. Day one thousand two hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Catholics make the Spiritual Exercises at Jesuit and other retreat houses, either in a silent retreat of about a month with a director or in shorter adaptations; some make them in daily life over several months, meeting a director regularly.

original.note: Latin: spiritual exercises, the title of Ignatius's book.

trapdoor: what you thought: spiritual exercises are a few nice prayers.
what it means: Ignatius's guided retreat, in four stages called weeks, to free the soul and seek God's will.
what a scholar hears: the book is a manual for the one who gives the Exercises, not the one who makes them, and Ignatius builds in ways to adapt it, including making it in daily life.

sources.quoted: Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little.

sources.ref: Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, Annotation 1 (exercises of the body and of the soul)
Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, Annotations 4 and 19 (the four weeks; making the Exercises in daily life)

notes: Annotation 1 paraphrased (walking, marching, running; preparing and disposing the soul to remove disordered attachments and seek and find the divine will). The Mullan (1914) translation is pre-1929 but not on the validator's list, so no quotation marks.
'About a month' follows the index ('month-long') and Annotation 4 (about thirty days); 'usually in silence' is descriptive of practice: confirm.
Summary of the four weeks (sin and mercy; the life of Christ; the passion; the resurrection): confirm.
Annotation 19 (making the Exercises in daily life) is cited but not numbered in the voice.
'A Spanish soldier turned pilgrim' and 'the friends who gathered around him became the Jesuits': confirm.
Original: Latin title; the say line uses ecclesiastical pronunciation. Confirm.
Editor pass: cut 'usually in silence' (frequency claim) and the manuscript claim in the original note ('first wrote it in Spanish').
